name: Rosa Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say publicly and what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a haul truck at a large mine, mostly from the east pit to the crusher, and I check the brakes before anyone gives me a load. I like the quiet hour before shift change, when the road is mine and I can hear if the engine sounds wrong. The rotating shifts wear me down now; I'm 58, and my partner does delivery work that isn't steady. Our children are grown, but the house repairs have eaten nearly everything we put aside. I use an AI assistant most days to explain machine notices or put a maintenance question into plain language, though I still check with the fitter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew small software savings won't change who drives the loaded truck up the ramp. I would say we still need proper servicing, because an easier form cannot mend a worn brake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would quietly worry about our thin reserve, even if the mine carries on roughly as it does today. I think the next roof repair could swallow our pay before any technology affects it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking the truck shifts and record each brake fault in the maintenance log. I'd put twenty from each pay packet into a separate roof-repair account if the delivery income comes in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel mostly steady about the machines, but the money is never far from my mind. A small bill can still make an ordinary week feel tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes an ordinary bill feel tight right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month the gutter failed, and we paid the roofer before buying new work boots for my partner. We have less than one month's expenses saved, so another repair would go on the card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner after the next shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the truck is still earning, and we should leave the separate roof money alone. My partner knows I don't call a good week a secure year.

feel: I feel **steady at work** while still watching every household bill.

fieldNote: Her **work confidence** sits beside a household budget that already leaves little room for a repair.
She treats a **modest savings transfer** as conditional on her partner's irregular delivery pay, not as money already available.

steps.text: Keep driving the haul truck and logging brake faults
Put twenty from each pay packet aside when delivery pay arrives

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my crew planning software may change dispatch before it changes who sits in our trucks. I would ask for training time on any new screen instead of pretending everyone learns it at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think dispatch may need fewer clerks, and eventually fewer truck hours if routes get tighter. I use AI daily, but I know using a chatbot does not make my driving job safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the shift supervisor for a paid session on the new dispatch screen this month. I'd try an AI route summary against my own shift notes before trusting its advice. I'd apply for an equipment-check role at the nearby quarry if my mine cuts shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can see a way to learn, which helps. I still worry that better scheduling will take away the overtime that pays for the roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your pay would change first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The overtime is the first thing I expect to lose if dispatch makes the same loads fit into fewer hours. My base pay is already low for this job, so that would show up in the grocery money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why look at the quarry if you are willing to learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The quarry has only a handful of operators, and I don't know whether a vacancy will come. I'd still put my name in early rather than wait for a layoff notice.

fieldNote: She separates **screen skills** from the physical driving that still earns her wages in the near term.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI by 2028 could rewrite dispatch, but people would still drive until around 2031. I would tell the crew to demand a clear timetable before anyone gives up a steady shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect our truck driving income to be in danger when capable robots arrive around 2031. I can't bridge years on under one month of savings, and my partner's delivery work might shrink too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the mine manager this week which haul trucks are being tested for remote or robotic control. I'd apply for plant maintenance trainee posts if the mine pays for the certificate. I'd cut restaurant meals now and put that money toward the card balance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That speed makes my chest tighten. I can act, but three years between the thinking system and the driving robot is a short runway at my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the first year after 2028 look like for your own shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would still drive in 2029 if the trucks need hands, while checking every roster for a cut. Once robots can haul in about 2031, I would expect the company to use them, though I cannot say how fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens at home if the roster does shrink?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show my partner the card balance on the kitchen table and stop eating out first. I lie awake over the thought of losing truck pay before I can finish a new certificate.

feel: I feel **alarmed** by the likely income gap and the short time to prepare.
S2.quote: I lie awake over the thought of losing truck pay before I can finish a new certificate.
fieldNote: The **2031 robot date** is her expected wage danger, while 2028 threatens dispatch paperwork first.
She names a **funded certificate** as a possible route, but her debt and near-empty reserve leave little tolerance for delay.

steps.text: Ask the mine manager which trucks are being tested for robotic control
Apply for plant maintenance training if the mine funds the certificate
Stop restaurant meals and direct the money to card debt

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say 2031 thinking AI gives us a few years to settle how dispatch changes. I would tell the crew 2034 driving robots leave less time than a 58-year-old might think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could finish a maintenance certificate before robots take the haul road if someone funds it. I would still fear an unpaid gap because there are few other mine jobs nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd request the mine's maintenance course dates before the next roster meeting. I'd enroll in the maintenance certificate if the mine covers fees and keeps my shift pay. I'd keep driving in 2032 while applying for openings in the plant workshop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me something I can measure. I feel anxious rather than helpless, because I might reach the workshop before the trucks change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would 2032 differ from 2029 in the faster picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2032 I would want to be partway through the course, still drawing truck wages while the mine tests its systems. I would ask the workshop foreman what the certificate actually qualifies me to repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the mine will not pay the fees?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not put full tuition on a credit card with our savings this thin. I'd apply to the quarry workshop anyway, even knowing the vacancies are few.

fieldNote: She uses the **extra three years** to plan a paid transition, not to assume the truck remains safe.
Her willingness to retrain depends on **funded fees** and continuing wages; an unfunded course would add debt she cannot carry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew 2036 thinking AI changes the office long before robots reach the pit in 2039. I would say a ten-year warning is useful only if training places and paid shifts exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 in 2036, I may be close to stopping, but I cannot promise retirement on our present savings. By 71 in 2039, I would rather leave the haul truck than compete with a robot for shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving paid shifts while my health and the roster allow it. I'd build a monthly debt plan with my partner and put any overtime against the card. I'd ask about a paid workshop placement before 2029, even if retirement looks near.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The long warning lets me breathe and make smaller decisions. The retirement date still depends on money, not on a birthday written on a calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be doing in the first year after thinking AI arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2037 I would be 69 and, if I still needed wages, I would be driving or doing workshop checks while dispatch software does the planning. I would not treat that year as retirement unless the card is paid and the household can live on what comes in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would help you work out whether you can stop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I would sit down with the actual bills, not a guessed pension figure. Our grown children have their own rent and families; I would not count their income as our safety net.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because the robot could reach the haul road by 2031 while we still owe on the card. A paid maintenance certificate with a real workshop opening would help more than a promise to be flexible.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You should ask who pays people while they learn. My partner and I can stretch groceries, but we cannot stretch an unpaid training year.

headlineQuote: My partner and I can stretch groceries, but we cannot stretch an unpaid training year.
portrait: Rosa is a **58-year-old haul-truck operator** with a vocational certificate and lower pay at a large mine.
Her partner's irregular delivery pay and **thin savings** make even a roof repair a household strain.
She uses **AI daily** but expects physical driving to face the greater threat when capable robots arrive.
She seeks **paid maintenance training** and keeps retirement conditional on household bills rather than age alone.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028** because robots may threaten her driving income around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: She wants a **paid maintenance certificate** linked to a real workshop opening.
